t.1.110.2: Pāṇḍu said: Alas, even those born in a family of the virtuous, if their selves are undisciplined and they are deluded by the net of desire, come to misfortune through their own deeds.
t.1.110.1: Having left behind the one who had died, as though he were his own kinsman, the king, together with his wife, stricken with grief and sorrow, lamented in his distress.
t.1.110.3: Though born of one whose soul was ever devoted to dharma, my father, while still a mere youth, reached the end of his life, being given over to desire. So we have heard.
t.1.110.4: In the field of that king whose soul was given over to desire, the seer of restrained speech, the blessed Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself, begot me.
t.1.110.5: Today this base mind of mine has fixed itself on vice, on hunting, wicked-souled as I am and forsaken by the gods because of my folly.
t.1.110.7: Therefore I, alone, a shaven-headed sage, will wander over this earth, living on alms, spending a single day beneath each tree.
t.1.110.6: I resolve upon liberation alone, O kinsman, for this is a great calamity. I shall follow that imperishable good conduct of my father, and without doubt I shall yoke myself to the most intense austerity.
t.1.110.8: Covered all over with dust, taking shelter in an empty house or making my dwelling at the foot of a tree, I shall have abandoned everything pleasant and unpleasant.
t.1.110.10: Never mocking anyone, never frowning anywhere, always serene of face, he delighted in the welfare of all beings.
t.1.110.11: Never harming anything of the fourfold creation, moving or unmoving, I shall always be impartial toward all living beings, as though they were my own children.
t.1.110.9: Neither grieving nor rejoicing, treating blame and praise of myself alike, I shall be without wishes, without salutations, free from the pairs of opposites, and without possessions.
t.1.110.12: Going about for alms only once a day, to two and five households, or, if no alms are to be had, even undertaking fasts.
t.1.110.15: Doing nothing like one who wishes to live, nor like one who wishes to die, neither welcoming death nor life, nor hating them.
t.1.110.13: Eating only a little at a time, whatever is fit to be eaten, sometimes from the very first alms received, never overstepping the rule when I receive, and when I receive nothing, completing the round of seven houses.
t.1.110.14: Whether one man hews off one of this body's arms and another anoints the other with sandalwood, I shall wish neither ill nor good to either of those two.
t.1.110.16: Whatever rites for worldly prosperity can be performed by one who is living, passing beyond them all, I shall abide in nothing more than the blinking of the eyes and such.
t.1.110.18: Freed from all sins, having passed beyond all snares, standing in the power of no one, I shall be like Mātariśvan, the wind.
t.1.110.19: Living constantly by this mode of life, of such a kind as this, I shall sustain my body, having set out upon the path that is free from fear.
t.1.110.17: In all those conditions I will have given up the workings of all the senses, my self having wholly renounced dharma, and the stains of my self thoroughly washed away.
t.1.110.20: Bereft of virility, I would find no delight in the path that dogs tread, a path fit for the powerless and the wretched, forever departed from one's own dharma.
t.1.110.22: Having spoken thus, the king, sorely stricken with grief and sighing deeply, looked at Kuntī and Mādrī and addressed them.
t.1.110.21: Whether honored or dishonored, the man ruled by desire who, with a piteous, beggarly gaze, resorts to another means of livelihood walks the path of dogs.
t.1.110.23: Kausalyā, Vidura the steward, the king together with his kinsmen, the noble Satyavatī, Bhīṣma, and those royal priests,
t.1.110.25: Having heard the words of their husband, whose mind was set on dwelling in the forest, Kuntī and Mādrī spoke words in accord with it.
t.1.110.24: And the great-souled brahmins who drink the soma and are rigorous in their vows, and the elders of the city who dwell there under our protection, all of them, after you have shown them due courtesy, must be told: “Pāṇḍu has gone forth into the forest as a renunciant.”
t.1.110.27: For we two, having restrained the host of our senses, intent on our husband's world, and having renounced the pleasures of desire, shall practise vast austerities.
t.1.110.26: There are other āśramas as well, O bull among the Bharatas, which can be undertaken together with us two, your lawful wives; having practised great austerity, you yourself will surely attain even heaven, there is no doubt.
t.1.110.28: If you abandon us two, O greatly wise one, O lord of the people, this very day we two shall give up our lives; of this there is no doubt.
t.1.110.30: Having abandoned the pleasures and practices of village life, practicing great austerity, clad in bark and eating fruits and roots, I shall wander in the great forest.
t.1.110.29: If this resolve of you two is indeed in keeping with dharma, then I shall follow that imperishable way of life that was my father's own.
t.1.110.31: Offering oblations into the fire at both times of day and bathing at both times of day, lean and sparing in food, I shall wear bark garments, a deerskin and matted locks.
t.1.110.32: Enduring cold, wind and heat, beset by hunger, thirst and weariness, I shall waste away this body with austerity hard to practise.
t.1.110.33: Given to solitude and deep reflection, sustaining myself on what is ripe and unripe, I shall satisfy the ancestors and the gods with forest fare, with words of prayer, and with water.
t.1.110.35: Thus, striving after the fierce and ever fiercer discipline of the forest scriptures, I shall remain so until this body of mine comes to its end.
t.1.110.34: Never doing anything displeasing even in the sight of the forest-dwelling hermits and of those who live in households, how much less in the sight of those who dwell in villages.
t.1.110.37: Having given everything away to the Brahmins, Pāṇḍu spoke again: "Having gone to Nāgapura, it should be said: 'Pāṇḍu has departed into the forest as a renunciant.'"
t.1.110.38: Abandoning everything, wealth, desire and pleasure, and delight of the highest kind, the bull among the Kurus set forth together with his wives.
t.1.110.36: Having spoken thus to those two wives, the king born of the Kaurava lineage then gave up his crest-jewel, his gold necklace, his two armlets and his earrings, his costly garments, and the ornaments of the women.
t.1.110.39: Then his retinue and those attendants, hearing the many piteous words of that lion of the Bharatas, raised a terrible cry of distress and wailed aloud, "Alas! Alas!"
t.1.110.40: Shedding hot tears, they left that lord of the earth and went swiftly to Nāgapura, taking with them all his words.
t.1.110.41: And having heard from them all that had happened in the great forest, just as it had occurred, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, best of men, grieved for Pāṇḍu alone.
t.1.110.42: Then the prince Pāṇḍu, the Kauravya, living on roots and fruits, went with his two wives to the mountain Nāgasabha.
t.1.110.43: He reached Caitraratha, passed beyond Vāriṣeṇa, and, crossing over the Himavant, went on to Gandhamādana.
t.1.110.44: Protected by the great beings, by the Siddhas and by the supreme seers, the king then dwelt there, on level ground and on rough alike.
t.1.110.45: Having reached Lake Indradyumna and passed beyond Haṃsakūṭa, he became an ascetic on Mount Śataśṛṅga, O great king.
